statement: Treat runners with no or little recent running history as the highest injury-risk class. Pooled incidence is 17.8 vs 7.7 per 1000 h of running (novice vs recreational), about 2.3 times per hour of exposure; use for classification and display, not as a causal hazard ratio.
appliesTo: Runners with no running in the prior several months or no running history

statement: Collect age, BMI, recent non-sport musculoskeletal complaints and running experience at intake. Set soft risk flags (slower start, more walk intervals) for age 45-65, BMI over 30, prior non-running musculoskeletal complaints and no running history. Do not use sex or previous running injury as modifiers. No flag should exclude anyone; no thresholds beyond those quoted are justified.
value: age 45-65; BMI > 30; prior non-sport MSK complaint; no running history

statement: Default weekly progression for novices is at most 10% per week of running time, with no more than about 30% growth over any 2-week window. Both numbers are conservative conventions: the 10% rule showed no injury benefit in an RCT and the 30% signal was not statistically significant. UI copy must not claim these prevent injury. At very low volumes use a small absolute minimum step (default one extra minute of running per week, grade D) rather than 10%.
value: 10% per week default; 30% over any 2 weeks as hard cap
unit: % change in weekly running time or distance
appliesTo: Novice runners and returning runners with a long layoff

statement: Flag (warn, not block) any logged week whose GPS distance is more than 30% above the prior 2-week level and cap the next planned week at the prior week's level. The evidence is an exploratory non-significant signal (HR 1.59, 95% CI 0.96-2.66) for distance-related overuse injuries.

Start novices with run-walk intervals on 3 non-consecutive days per week for the first 6 weeks (NLstart2run program length), lengthening run intervals before walk intervals shrink. No trial establishes injury benefit or the best ratio. Use a conservative, configurable default of short run intervals (about 1 minute) with longer walk intervals; label the ratio grade D.
value: 3 sessions/week, non-consecutive; 6-week run-walk phase; ratio default about 1:2 (unvalidated)
unit: sessions per week; weeks; run:walk ratio
appliesTo: Novice runners and runners restarting after a long layoff or after a bone stress injury

statement: Include a hip and core strength block before novice running sessions. In an RCT it reduced lower-extremity injury incidence (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.45-0.97) and weekly overuse-injury prevalence (PRR 0.61). The abstract gives no set, rep or frequency; use configurable defaults and label them grade D. Do not offer ankle/foot-only routines as prevention (no benefit, more acute injuries in the trial).
value: include before runs; dose not established (default 2-3 sessions/week, grade D)

statement: Progress either high-intensity running time or total weekly volume in a block, not both at once. Trial data show no difference in specific injury types between intensity-focused and volume-focused progression, so no separate injury-risk model is justified. Treat an 8-week low-intensity preconditioning phase as a conservative option for new runners; its benefit is not tested.
value: one variable at a time; optional 8-week preconditioning

statement: Offer a run/walk strategy as an option for marathon goals: similar finish time (about +6:45 mean, not significant) with less post-race muscle pain and fatigue. Do not claim cardiac protection. Do not extrapolate walk ratios or benefits to 50 km-100 mile events.
value: available; expect about +7 min vs continuous running; no cardiac benefit claim

statement: Model aerobic fitness loss during a layoff as saturating: about 7% VO2max by 3 weeks and up to about 16% by 8 weeks in long-trained athletes, flattening after roughly 30-60 days. Cap modelled loss at about 15-20% for long-trained runners. Scale decay up for higher VO2max and under-20s. Recently trained runners (gains of a few months) lose all of those gains after more than 4 weeks. Re-estimate paces from fresh data after any break of 2 weeks or more.
value: 7% at day 21; 16% at day 56; plateau; cap 15-20%
appliesTo: Any runner returning after 2 or more weeks with no or minimal training

statement: Restart after a layoff at a fraction of prior volume and rebuild with the normal progression caps. The evidence supports direction, not magnitudes: under 7 days no reduction; 7-14 days about 90%; 15-28 days about 75%; over 28 days about 50-60%, with run-walk if the runner had under about 6 months of consistent running before the break. These fractions are conservative engineering defaults (grade D). Strength sessions can resume closer to prior loads than running volume.
appliesTo: Runners returning from a layoff of non-injury cause
evidenceLevel: mujika and coyle indicate direction only

statement: Maintenance mode: about 2 runs per week, weekly volume cut 33-66% (sessions of at least 13-26 min), at least one session at the usual intensity, and 1 strength session per week at 1 set per exercise (2 sessions and 2-3 sets for older runners). Limit to about 15 weeks by default, then re-check fitness and notify the runner. Add a visible caveat that ultra-specific durability and race-specific endurance are not covered.
value: 2 runs/week; volume -33% to -66%; session >= 13-26 min; intensity kept; max about 15 weeks
unit: runs per week; % volume; minutes; weeks
appliesTo: Time-limited reduced-availability periods in general-population runners

statement: When a break is not medically required, prescribe a small number of easy sessions (default 1-2 per week, same mode where possible) rather than complete rest; any exercise weakens detraining. For injuries that forbid running, substitute cross-training.
value: 1-2 easy sessions per week (default, grade D value)
appliesTo: Runners on planned or forced breaks without a contraindication to exercise

statement: On a logged bone stress injury, set the earliest return-to-run date by site using pooled return-to-sport times: posteromedial tibial shaft 44 days, fibula 56 days, femoral neck 107 days, tarsal navicular 127 days. Use as minimum planning intervals (they are average return-to-sport times, not run-specific). Treat femoral neck, tarsal navicular, anterior tibial shaft and fifth metatarsal as high risk requiring clinician clearance.
appliesTo: Athletes with a logged bone stress injury

statement: Do not generate running sessions after a tibial bone stress injury until the runner confirms: no bony tenderness, pain-free walking, and, for high-risk sites, clinician clearance (a clinician-entered date). Then start a graduated walk-run programme, increase running distance before speed or intensity, and hold progression when symptoms recur. Interval lengths and step sizes are not evidenced: use conservative grade D defaults.
value: 3 athlete-confirmed criteria plus clinician date for high-risk sites; distance before intensity
appliesTo: Runners returning after tibial bone stress injury (apply cautiously to other lower-limb bone stress injuries)
